title: The heart of the sun
hook: a sage with a hymn to the sun, heads that grow back, and one last arrow
carry: turn to the sun: the aditya hridayam

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lakshmana took a spear meant for Vibhishana, keeping Rama's vow of refuge, and Matali brought Indra's chariot down. Sharanagati: whoever comes for refuge is safe.

The duel has gone on so long that Rama is worn out. He stands in Indra's chariot, tired to the bone, with Ravana in front of him ready to fight again. And in that pause, Valmiki says, the sage Agastya, who had come with the gods to watch, walks up to Rama on the battlefield: the same sage who gave Rama weapons years ago in the forest. This time he doesn't bring a weapon. He brings a hymn.
screen: `WORN OUT.` → `AGASTYA WALKS UP.` → `NOT A WEAPON. A HYMN.`

segments.voice: It's called the Aditya Hridayam, the heart of the sun, a hymn praising the sun as the source of light and life. Agastya teaches it to Rama there and then, and tells him to recite it three times. Rama does, facing the sun, and Valmiki says his weariness lifts and his heart fills with courage. Hindus have honored the sun as a face of the divine since the Vedas: Surya, who gives light and life to everything. Many still greet it at dawn, some with this very hymn, some by pouring a little water toward it, an offering called arghya. Then the fight resumes, and it's terrifying. Rama cuts off one of Ravana's heads, and another grows in its place. Again and again, Valmiki says, a hundred times. Matali, the charioteer, reminds Rama of the weapon of Brahma, given to him long ago by Agastya. Rama takes it up. It blazes like the fire at the end of time. He charges it with the proper mantra, draws his bow to the full, and lets it go. The arrow strikes Ravana in the chest, and he falls from his chariot. The gods rain flowers. On Dussehra, also called Vijayadashami, towns in North India set giant effigies of Ravana alight to mark this victory. In the book, the moment is quieter: a tired man turns to the sun, and then one arrow.
screen: `THE HEART OF THE SUN.` · `SURYA: GIVER OF LIGHT AND LIFE.` · `ARGHYA: WATER FOR THE RISING SUN.` · `RAVANA FALLS.` · then, large: `A TIRED MAN TURNS TO THE SUN.`

segments.voice: If you can, face a window or wherever the sun is. Many Hindus greet the sun at dawn with folded hands, or a little water poured toward it. If you pray, offer a few words of thanks to the sun, giver of light, in your own way. If you don't, simply stand in the light, name your tiredness honestly, the way Rama faced his, and let the light hold it for a moment.
Aditya Hridayam. The hymn to the sun that Agastya teaches Rama, lifting his weariness before the weapon of Brahma ends the war.
Your line: turn to the sun, the Aditya Hridayam. When the noise dies down, someone comes out of the city to grieve. Day six hundred fifty-five, done.

howItsDone: Devotees recite the Aditya Hridayam, especially at sunrise, and on Dussehra (Vijayadashami) Ramlila performances in North India end with Ravana's effigy being burned.

Agastya.meaning: the sage who gave Rama weapons and now a hymn

Dussehra.meaning: the autumn festival marking Rama's victory over Ravana

arghya.meaning: an offering of water, often poured toward the rising sun

Surya.meaning: the sun, honored as a god since the Vedas

recall: right living, duty and truth in one word
